Case Based Reasoning using Statistical Models

The R package CaseBasedReasoning implements case-based reasoning with statistical and machine learning models: it learns a distance between cases from a fitted regression model or random forest, retrieves the most similar past cases, predicts outcomes (including survival curves) from them, and explains why cases match.

Introduction: What is Case Based Reasoning?

Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) is an artificial intelligence (AI) and problem-solving methodology that leverages the knowledge and experience gained from previously encountered situations, known as cases, to address new and complex problems. CBR relies on the principle that similar problems often have similar solutions, and it focuses on identifying, adapting, and reusing those solutions to solve new problems.

The CBR process consists of four main steps:

  • Retrieve: In this step, the system searches its case database to identify the most similar cases to the current problem. It uses similarity measures and pattern matching techniques to compare the features of the new problem with the existing cases.

  • Reuse: Once the relevant cases are retrieved, the system adapts the solutions from those cases to fit the new problem. This may involve combining multiple solutions, adjusting parameters, or modifying the solution to accommodate any differences between the old and new cases.

  • Revise: After the adapted solution has been applied to the new problem, the system evaluates the outcome to determine its effectiveness. If necessary, the solution is further revised and optimized to better suit the specific context of the problem.

  • Retain: Finally, the new problem and its corresponding solution are added to the case database for future reference. This step enhances the system’s knowledge base and improves its ability to solve similar problems in the future.

CBR has been successfully applied in various domains, including medical diagnosis, legal reasoning, customer support, and design optimization. Its ability to learn from experience and adapt to new situations makes it a valuable approach in fields where expertise and problem-solving skills are crucial.

How This Package Implements CBR

The central challenge in CBR is defining what “similar” means. This package solves the Retrieve step by learning a distance function from data rather than relying on ad-hoc similarity measures.

The workflow follows three stages:

  1. Fit a statistical model to the training data. The model captures which variables matter and how strongly they influence the outcome.
  2. Derive a distance function from the fitted model. The model’s structure determines how distance between cases is measured.
  3. Retrieve the k nearest cases for each new query observation using the learned distance.

The package offers two families of models for this:

Regression-based distance (Cox, linear, logistic)

A regression model (Cox proportional hazards, OLS, or logistic regression via the rms package) is fitted on the training data. The estimated regression coefficients are then used as weights in a weighted absolute distance function. Variables with larger coefficients contribute more to the distance, while variables the model deems irrelevant contribute little. This follows the approach of Dippon et al. (2002).

Distances are computed in contribution space: for each model term t, the contribution to the linear predictor, c_t(x) = X_t(x) %*% beta_t, is compared between two cases, and the absolute differences are summed. For main effects this is exactly the weighted distance above; it also covers any other rms term, such as splines (rcs(age, 4)), polynomials and interactions.

Random Forest distance (proximity and depth)

A random forest (via the ranger package) is fitted on the training data. Two distance measures can be extracted:

  • Proximity distance: Two observations are similar if they frequently land in the same terminal node across trees; the distance is sqrt(1 - proximity). Besides Breiman’s original proximity, the out-of-bag (OOB) proximity and RF-GAP (Rhodes, Cutler & Moon, 2023) are available. RF-GAP removes the in-bag bias of the original measure: the RF-GAP weighted average of the training outcomes reproduces the forest’s prediction.
  • Depth distance (default): The distance between two observations is the sum of edges between their terminal nodes across all trees in the forest, following Englund and Verikas (2012). Unlike proximity, it distinguishes cases that end up in neighbouring leaves from cases in distant parts of the tree.

Both approaches produce an (n x m) distance matrix, where n is the number of training observations and m the number of query observations. This matrix can be used directly for clustering or visualization, or passed to the built-in k-nearest-neighbor search to retrieve the most similar cases.

Installation

CRAN 

install.packages("CaseBasedReasoning")

GITHUB 

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("sipemu/case-based-reasoning")

Features

  • Models: linear, logistic and Cox regression (with splines and interactions), and random forests (ranger) for numeric, binary, multi-class and survival endpoints.
  • Distances: regression-weighted (contribution-space) distance; random forest proximity (original, OOB, RF-GAP) and depth distance; all implemented in parallel C++.
  • Retrieval: get_similar_cases() / predict() return the k nearest training cases per query, optionally merged with the query and excluding the query itself (exclude_self = TRUE).
  • Survival prediction: predict_survival() estimates a Kaplan–Meier curve from each query’s nearest cases; evaluate_survival() scores it with Uno’s C-index and the integrated Brier score.
  • Counterfactuals: get_counterfactual_cases() returns the most similar cases with a different outcome.
  • Explanations: explain_match() shows which variables make two cases similar or different.
  • Checks: query data are validated against the training data (factor levels are matched by name, unknown levels and missing values are errors), and check_ph() checks the proportional hazards assumption of the Cox model.

Missing Values

Training cases with missing values in the endpoint or the predictors are dropped when the model is fitted, with a warning that lists them. They are excluded consistently from fitting, distance calculation and retrieval. Missing values in a query are an error, so impute them or remove those cases first.

Example: Cox Beta Model

Initialization

In the first example, we use the CPH model and the ovarian data set from the survival package. In the first step, we initialize the R6 data object.

library(survival)
library(CaseBasedReasoning)
ovarian$resid.ds <- factor(ovarian$resid.ds)
ovarian$rx <- factor(ovarian$rx)
ovarian$ecog.ps <- factor(ovarian$ecog.ps)

# initialize R6 object
cph_model <- CoxModel$new(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ age + resid.ds + rx + ecog.ps, data = ovarian)

Similar Cases

After the initialization, we may want to get for each case in the query data the most similar case from the learning data.

n <- nrow(ovarian)
trainID <- sample(1:n, floor(0.8 * n), FALSE)
testID <- (1:n)[-trainID]
cph_model <- CoxModel$new(Surv(futime, fustat) ~ age + resid.ds + rx + ecog.ps, data = ovarian[trainID, ])

# fit model
cph_model$fit()

# get similar cases
matched_tbl <- cph_model$get_similar_cases(query = ovarian[testID, ], k = 3)

# or use the standard S3 predict interface
matched_tbl <- predict(cph_model, newdata = ovarian[testID, ], k = 3)

To analyze the results, you can extract the similar cases and training data and combine them:

  • Note 1: Training cases with missing values are dropped when the model is fitted (see Missing Values).

  • Note 2: The data.frame returned from cph_model$get_similar_cases() contains the matched training cases, k rows per query, with additional columns:

    • scDist: The distance between the query and the matched case.

    • caseId: Rank of the match for its query (1 = most similar, …, k).

    With merge = TRUE, the query cases are included as well, and two more columns identify them:

    • scCaseId: Number of the query case; a query and its matches share the same value.

    • group: "Query" or "Matched".

Distance Matrix

The distance matrix is a square matrix that represents the pairwise distances between a set of data points. In the context of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR), the distance matrix captures the dissimilarities between cases in the training and test (or query) datasets, based on the fitted model and the values of the predictor variables.

The distance matrix can be helpful in various situations:

  • Identifying Similar Cases: By examining the distance matrix, you can identify the most similar cases to a given query case. Smaller distances indicate higher similarity, enabling the retrieval of relevant cases for CBR.

  • Clustering and Grouping: The distance matrix can be used as input for clustering algorithms, such as hierarchical clustering or k-means clustering, to group cases with similar characteristics. This can provide insights into the structure and patterns within the data.

  • Visualizing Relationships: By creating a heatmap of the distance matrix, you can visualize the relationships between cases. This representation can help identify trends and anomalies in the data, guiding further analysis and decision-making.

  • Model Validation: The distance matrix can be used to assess the performance of the CPH regression model or other statistical models employed in the CBR process. Comparing the distance matrix for different models can help determine which model better captures the relationships between cases.

In summary, a distance matrix can provide valuable insights into the relationships between cases, facilitate the identification of similar cases for CBR, and aid in the validation of the chosen statistical models.

distance_matrix <- cph_model$calc_distance_matrix()

cph_model$calc_distance_matrix() calculates the distance matrix between train and test data. When test data is omitted, the distances between observations in the training data are calculated. Rows are observations in train and columns observations of test. The distance matrix is saved internally in the CoxModel object: cph_model$dist_matrix.

Beyond Retrieval

Survival prediction

For survival endpoints, the retrieved cases yield a prediction: a Kaplan–Meier estimate over each query’s k nearest training cases (Lowsky et al., 2013). evaluate_survival() scores the predictions on held-out data with Uno’s C-index and the integrated Brier score, so k and the distance method can be tuned. The ovarian test set above is too small for that, so we use lung:

lung_df <- na.omit(lung[, c("time", "status", "age", "sex", "ph.ecog", "wt.loss")])
lung_df$status <- lung_df$status - 1
lung_df$sex <- factor(lung_df$sex)
train <- sample(nrow(lung_df), 150)

lung_model <- CoxModel$new(Surv(time, status) ~ rcs(age, 3) + sex + ph.ecog + wt.loss,
                           lung_df[train, ])
lung_model$fit()

# survival probabilities at 1 and 2 years: one row per query
lung_model$predict_survival(lung_df[-train, ], k = 30, times = c(365, 730))

# Uno's C-index and integrated Brier score on test data
lung_model$evaluate_survival(lung_df[-train, ], k = 30)

Counterfactual cases and explanations

get_counterfactual_cases() returns the most similar training cases whose outcome differs from the query’s (Keane & Smyth, 2020). For survival endpoints, the outcome is the event status at horizon. explain_match() breaks a distance down: per model term for regression models, and per split variable at which the tree paths diverge for random forests.

query <- ovarian[testID[1], ]
cph_model$get_counterfactual_cases(query, k = 2, horizon = 365)

match <- cph_model$get_similar_cases(query, k = 1)
cph_model$explain_match(query, match)

Example: Random Forest 

rf_model <- RFModel$new(Species ~ ., data = iris, num.trees = 500)
rf_model$fit()

# default: depth distance
rf_model$get_similar_cases(iris[c(1, 51, 101), ], k = 3)

# RF-GAP proximity
rf_model$set_distance_method("Proximity", proximity_type = "rfgap")
rf_model$get_similar_cases(iris[c(1, 51, 101), ], k = 3)

# which variables separate two flowers in the forest?
rf_model$explain_match(iris[51, ], iris[60, ])

RF-GAP proximities are normalised to sum to one over the training cases, so RF-GAP distances lie close to 1; only their order matters for retrieval.
